abstract: Genome-resolved metagenomics is widely used to characterize activated sludge microbiomes and infer the microbial processes underpinning system performance. However, the reliability of metabolic inferences drawn from fragmented short-read (SR) genomes remains insufficiently examined. Using (near-)complete genomes reconstructed from HiFi long-read (LR) sequencing as references, we traced genome recovery through SR assembly and post-assembly processing. Assembly fragmentation and subsequent sequence loss during post-assembly processing compromised the recovery of high-quality genomes despite adequate sequencing depth and breadth of coverage. This incomplete recovery biased inferences regarding denitrification modularity, underestimating complete denitrifier populations and distorting the inferred balance between N2O producers and reducers. Poor recovery of nitrifier and Ca. Accumulibacter genomes, exacerbated by population microdiversity and structurally complex genomic regions, precluded reliable inferences regarding nitrification and phosphorus accumulation. Our findings caution against uncritical interpretation of SR-based microbiome-function linkages and highlight the value of incorporating HiFi LR sequencing into genome-resolved metagenomic analyses.
